Every song that you hear on a singing show has been through my desk. My job is rights clearance. When a contestant chooses a song, a request is sent to the publisher, and the song is cleared only when the permission comes back in writing. Most requests are answered in a week. Some are never answered at all. Last season, a song was chosen for the semi-final on a Monday, and the permission was refused on Thursday, two days before the show. The singer was told that night. A new song was chosen, a new arrangement was written in twenty-four hours, and the band rehearsed it on Friday morning. On Saturday it was sung live, and nobody watching at home knew that it was the second choice. People think the hard part of television is the cameras. For me, the hard part is a piece of paper that is signed by somebody I have never met.

I edit a ninety-minute episode, and I start with about ten hours of footage. That means that almost everything that is recorded is never seen. People ask me if that is sad. It is not. It is the job. On a live show, the footage is recorded by fifteen cameras, and every camera is logged by an assistant while the show is happening. By Sunday morning the best moments are marked, and the first version is cut by Sunday night. Then it is watched by the producers, and they always ask for the same thing: shorter. Whole performances are cut because they arrive at the wrong moment in the story. The hardest one I ever cut was a duet which was perfect. It was simply too long, and it was removed in the last version. The singers never asked me about it. I think they never knew how well it was filmed.

The format was bought from the company that created it. Singers were found in auditions all over the country. Every song was cleared before the first rehearsal. The call sheet was sent to the crew the night before. Hours of footage were recorded by fifteen cameras. The episode was edited, and it aired on Saturday night.
